slides.heading: Motivation
slides.text: Consider dicing a carrot versus a radish. The objects differ, but the skill and the change from start to goal are the same. Good representations are invariant to irrelevant details and equivariant to what varies. Prior bisimulation handled distractors for one task; we lift it to families of tasks.

slides.heading: Contribution
slides.text: The paper makes three contributions. It defines goal-conditioned bisimulation, grouping state-goal pairs that behave equivalently. It gives a metric-learning objective so new goals arise from latent arithmetic. And it proves the representation is sufficient for any state-only reward task.

slides.heading: Method
slides.text: GCB learns two encoders together. Phi encodes a state-goal pair so its L1 distance matches an on-policy bisimulation metric, capturing how differently two tasks behave. Psi encodes a state so the goal embedding minus the state embedding equals phi. That makes goals composable: add an analogous pair to your state, then take the nearest neighbor in psi space. Training is offline on Implicit Q-Learning.

slides.heading: Takeaway
slides.text: The takeaway: treating bisimulation as an equivalence over tasks, not just states, aligns analogous tasks in one space. Because goals become composable by arithmetic, you can point a robot at an example and have it infer its own goal, provably sufficient for any state-only reward task.
